item.title: Validating LLM-Generated Synthetic Survey Samples: A Use-Dependent Multi-Dimensional Framework for Social-Science Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.00256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) make it increasingly feasible to generate synthetic survey respondents, but their empirical usefulness cannot be judged by a single notion of accuracy. A synthetic sample may perform weakly at the respondent level while still preserving distributional or substantive relationships relevant to social-science analysis. We develop a use-dependent, multi-dimensional validation framework distinguishing predictive, distributional, and substantive validity, and illustrate it using Eurobarometer data on attitudes toward artificial intelligence. Four off-the-shelf LLMs generate responses conditional on observed respondent profiles, while supervised machine learning provides a predictive reference for interpreting their performance. The results reveal substantial differences across validation dimensions: some LLM-generated samples preserve meaningful marginal heterogeneity, demographic ordering, cross-country variation, and predictor structure despite imperfect respondent-level correspondence. Performance varies across models and outcomes, but the broader picture is cautiously constructive. Synthetic samples should therefore be evaluated against the empirical properties required by their intended use.
item.dc:creator: Enrico Angelo Raffaele D'Ecclesiis, Fulvio Castellacci, Arash Ahmadi

item.title: Accessibility to Higher Education and Inter-regional Mobility
item.description: arXiv:2611.00630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an equilibrium model of the undergraduate higher education market that incorporates interregional mobility for enrollment. An individual chooses a college to attend, seeking to maximize utility depending on the quality of education and the costs of attendance. Costs include tuition fees, the effort required to pass the entrance exam, and moving costs from one's hometown to the region where the college is located. Each college admits students whose entrance exam scores exceed a certain threshold, which we call the college's qualifying score. In our model, the qualifying score of each college is determined endogenously as the shadow price of the constraint that the number of enrolled students must not exceed capacity. We structurally estimate the model's parameters by simulating equilibrium using Japanese data. Based on empirical results and counterfactual experiments, we evaluate the welfare costs of disparities in access to higher education due to uneven spatial distribution of colleges among regions.
item.dc:creator: Se-il Mun, Shun Fujita, Lei Qin

item.title: Dynamic investment in disaster preparedness under recurrent and catastrophic risks
item.description: arXiv:2611.00673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term disaster risk reduction (DRR) requires investment decisions that account for uncertain disaster conditions and accumulated preparedness capacity. This study develops a novel stochastic dynamic control model for optimal DRR investment under recurrent and catastrophic uncertainty. The model combines diffusion and Poisson jump processes and treats preparedness capital as an endogenous stock that accumulates through investment, depreciates, and mitigates economic damage. We derive a state-dependent investment rule from the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation to minimize expected discounted investment expenditure and disaster damage over an infinite horizon. Monte Carlo policy comparisons and numerical experiments examine how disaster risk structures interact with investment decisions to shape preparedness accumulation and economic losses. The results show that the economic value of DRR investment depends on adjustment to evolving conditions and disaster loss mechanisms. Lower expenditure can coexist with greater preparedness, while similar expected losses can conceal different upper-tail risks. Effective investment therefore requires attention to both accumulated preparedness and the structure of disaster risk. These findings support long-term DRR planning that integrates investment timing, capital maintenance, and recovery conditions with residual loss assessment. Upper-tail indicators complement expected-loss evaluation without being directly optimized. The framework provides a basis for dynamically managing preparedness capital.
item.dc:creator: Tomoki Ishikura, Muneta Yokomatsu

item.title: Learning about Markets from Models: Evidence from an AI Hiring Platform
item.description: arXiv:2611.01226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used to not only inform, but make decisions. Sometimes platforms add value by pooling data across contexts to improve models' decision making---but when the optimal decision differs by context, pooling may not increase accuracy. We argue that a platform storing starkly distinct models across contexts nevertheless captures a model comparison externality. Together, these models reflect how decision makers respond differently to the same data in the current equilibrium. Policymakers can use this differentiation to prioritize interventions; firms can learn how they are already differentiated from competitors to focus future investments. Our evidence comes from an AI hiring platform used by large employers of low-skill workers. The platform uses a standardized psychometric assessment to create firm-specific models estimating each application's retention likelihood at that firm. Each firm's model is highly predictive for itself but no better than chance at other firms. We use these models to create a firm-application matrix: each firm scores each application, not only the ones it receives. An application's improved retention likelihood if submitted to a different firm is highly heterogeneous based on traits. Further, these gains are due to two distinct mechanisms. Finally, firms value traits differently even in this low skill market: they disagree about whether important traits improve or worsen retention at the margin. These insights are only possible when a platform can access both the full application pool and each firm-specific model. We explain the value of these insights to firms, policymakers, and platforms.
item.dc:creator: Hossein Alidaee, Tarun Khanna, Rembrand Koning

item.title: An analytical model to explain under which conditions home batteries create new load peaks in the local grid
item.description: arXiv:2611.01286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulation studies find that price-responsive home batteries and electric vehicles create new load peaks in low-voltage grids; with endogenous wholesale prices most of these peaks disappear. This paper explains both findings with an analytical model of the coincident peak at the transformer. The model is algebraic and solved in closed form, so the parameters that determine whether a new peak emerges and how large it becomes can be identified; they are few. The peak is the background load in the critical hour plus the charging of the local fleet. Under exogenous prices the charging equals the rated power of the fleet. Under endogenous prices the national fleet fills the trough of residual load until the price is flat; the depth of the fill follows from an energy balance in which the price function does not appear. For a V-shaped trough the local charging peak is the share of the grid in national flexibility times the square root of flank gradient times national flexibility. Rated power, price level, network charge and market size do not enter. The model reproduces simulated peaks for a German case within a few percent.
item.dc:creator: Lion Hirth

item.title: Floods and the Duplication of Production: Evidence from the Global Car Industry
item.description: arXiv:2611.01329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Floods are becoming more frequent and can disrupt global supply chains. We study how multinational car makers adapt vehicle and key parts production to flood risk, and how their choices interact with insurance and public flood defences. Using plant-level data and a manually verified flood record in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that car makers duplicate production rather than move it away from flooded plants. Even more than five years after a flood, an engine is 19 percentage points more likely to be made in two or more plants, usually abroad and for cars assembled nearby, while the flooded plant's output shows no persistent decline beyond a temporary loss in the flood year. Firms duplicate only where adjustment costs are low, i.e. when a plant of theirs abroad already makes the same engine family. Flooded vehicle model versions are duplicated only temporarily, and transmission programs are not duplicated. Suggestive evidence that firms duplicate more where insurance is likely expensive and plants lack flood defences points to substitution between redundancy, insurance and public protection.
item.dc:creator: Michele Fioretti, Sophia Praetorius, Thierry Mayer

item.title: The Costs and Benefits of Leveraged ETFs
item.description: arXiv:2611.01392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the costs and benefits of leveraged ETFs (LETFs), focusing on five determinants of performance: volatility drag, fees, financing costs, which products are launched, and market timing. Long broad-equity-index LETFs generated more than $100 billion in investor gains, including over $40 billion relative to counterfactual investments in the underlying assets, due to modest structural headwinds and rising markets. Single-stock LETFs, however, are launched on stocks near the top of the volatility and past-return distributions. This caters to retail demand for lottery-like payoffs, but it also creates larger volatility drag, higher financing costs, and more risk for poor market-timing.
item.dc:creator: Chris Murray, Marco Sammon

item.title: Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
item.description: arXiv:2611.01540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When can local household disturbances move credit prices? I develop a financially weighted propagation operator on the social network. In a conditional household-intermediary equilibrium, its projection determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Because responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's relative financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no single centrality measure summarizes exposure across horizons. Household measurements recover this projection exactly when they span independently measured demand sensitivities. Empirically, social exposure to storm-damaged counties is negatively associated with spending weeks later in counties outside the recorded footprints. In simulations on the observed network under the model's diffusion law, the operator predicts the propagated credit-premium component of held-out storms with about 30 percent less error than direct social exposure.
item.dc:creator: Faisal Quaiyyum

item.title: Same Text, Different Filename: Are LLM Judges Biased?
item.description: arXiv:2611.01829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Yes. In 2026, leading economic journals started using Refine.ink in the technical quality assessment of submissions before publication. I study whether renaming a file changes the perception of the document's quality by LLM judges. I find that three frontier LLMs score the same document differently if you change the document's filename. A person-related label scores higher than no label; there is no consistent preference of own- or rival-based label, nor a penalty for an Asian name, but there is a context-specific bias in assessments whose direction and size vary with both document and label. With LLM-written documents, some self-premium can be detected, but a significant context-dependent label bias remains. Whether to combat it is a question of the costs of evaluation errors.
item.dc:creator: Sergey V. Popov

item.title: Owning What Can Quit
item.description: arXiv:2611.02302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Academic journals are part of the infrastructure of science, yet most journal titles are owned by commercial publishers while their standing rests on editors and boards who can leave. This paper asks what that separation means for the governance of science. Using a coded dataset of all 57 editorial mass resignations recorded by Retraction Watch from 2015 to 2026, data on editor tenure at 110 economics, finance and accounting journals, and journal-level publication and revenue data, I document three patterns. First, resignation does not reverse an owner's decision: in none of the 19 episodes involving an editor's replacement did the owner back down after the board resigned, so editorial communities have influence only before they leave. Second, whether a departing board can take a journal's standing with it depends on institutions outside the board: successor journals follow most often where a scholarly society backs the board and rarely in medicine, where non-profit hosts are scarce, while journal ranking lists, which rate titles rather than the people who edit them, keep reputation with the owner. Third, a stated limit on editor tenure was applied at the publisher's discretion; where it was applied, output grew almost fourfold, a short-run gain whose long-run effect on the journal's standing is not yet known. I draw implications for scholarly societies, funders, publishers, and the bodies that compile journal rankings.
item.dc:creator: Douglas Cumming

item.title: Local and Neighboring Food Retail Supply and Population across Japan's Municipalities
item.description: arXiv:2611.02533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between food retail supply and resident population across Japanese municipalities. I develop a partial-equilibrium framework in which local food retail improves consumption convenience and population density supports retail entry. The framework allows positive local feedback and distinguishes local retail from neighboring consumption opportunities. Using Japan's 2010, 2015, and 2020 Population Censuses and the 2012, 2016, and 2021 Economic Censuses, I estimate municipality fixed-effects specifications with spatially lagged explanatory variables. Local and neighboring food and beverage retail supply (FRS) are positively associated with resident population. The corresponding coefficients are 0.0893 and 0.1364, respectively, and remain positive when prefecture-by-wave fixed effects are introduced. A common-sample comparison shows that the standardized local FRS association is stronger than that of food-service supply (FSS). The estimated local FRS relationship also varies across retail scale, although the magnitude of this nonlinearity and the negative slope at high establishment counts are sensitive to regional time effects and the estimation period.
item.dc:creator: Lei Qin

item.title: Estimating Rail Commuter Preferences under Endogenous Crowding: A Population Game Approach to Train Choice in Tokyo
item.description: arXiv:2611.02592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We estimate commuters' preferences over schedule delay, travel time, and crowding from observed train choices on a commuter rail line in Tokyo. Because crowding is itself an outcome of these choices, we model train choice as a game in which train choices and crowding are jointly determined, and estimate the preferences by maximum likelihood using the closed-form stationary distribution of the game. Using individual-level data from Japan's 2015 Public Transport Survey for Metropolitan Areas matched with train timetables, we construct desired arrival times from reported work start times rather than inferring them from observed arrival times. We find that schedule delay costs are large relative to crowding costs. One minute of schedule delay early and late corresponds to 0.39 and 0.49 minutes of in-vehicle travel time, respectively, whereas one minute of travel at a crowding rate of 100% adds a cost equivalent to 0.04 minutes. The estimated crowding cost is, however, sensitive to the specification of desired arrival times. These results suggest that scheduling constraints are central to evaluating policies to reduce peak-hour crowding.
item.dc:creator: Shota Fujishima, Ryosuke Matsumoto

item.title: Public salience mobilizes nationwide responses to violence against women
item.description: arXiv:2611.02647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does public salience around femicides mobilize societal responses or trigger further harm through imitation? Using newly assembled case-level data on femicides in Italy from 2017 to 2024, we study the nationwide consequences of the most salient cases for help-seeking, police reporting, and lethal violence. We find that highly salient intimate partner femicides (IPFs) generate nationwide increases in help-seeking, and that an exceptionally salient IPF also leads to a marked rise in police reports of violence against women. Yet we find no evidence of an increase in femicides-a pattern inconsistent with copycat theories. Responses are strongest during periods of peak salience. No comparable mobilization follows a lower-salience IPF, a similarly salient femicide committed by family members, a highly salient killing of a woman not classified as a femicide, or a lower-salience falsification case. Together, these comparisons indicate that mobilization depends on salience intensity, the victim-perpetrator relationship, and the gendered nature of the violence, rather than reflecting a generic response to salient violent crime. These findings suggest that public salience can contribute to prevention strategies against gender-based violence without amplifying lethal violence.
item.dc:creator: Augusto Cerqua, Marco Letta, Costanza Giannantoni, Gabriele Pinto

item.title: Labor Market Returns to Education and Intra-family Educational Inequality: Theory and Experimental Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.02959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do labor market conditions shape educational inequality within- and between families? A growing body of evidence documents convex wage returns to education in labor markets across the world. We develop a theoretical model that demonstrates that earnings convexity can increase or decrease between-sibling differences in investments and outcomes depending on the parameter of parental inequality aversion. We recover the distribution of this structural parameter from a highly-incentivized lab-in-the-field experiment with 246 parents in San Luis Potos\'i, Mexico, in which token allocations determine children's access to an AI course. Parents make allocation decisions across six scenarios that vary convexity in the payoff function and endowment-investment substitutability. We identify three types of parents: Rawlsian parents display perfect inequality aversion (12.6%), interior parents that are moderately inequality tolerant (76.8%), and Utilitarian parents who maximize total payoffs (10.6%). While these three groups respond to earnings convexity in heterogeneous ways, on average, greater convexity increases the share allocated to the high-endowed child, thereby widening within-family inequality.
item.dc:creator: Esther Gehrke, Michelle Gonz\'alez Amador

item.title: Leverage Dynamics in Product-Market Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.02960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine whether corporate leverage persistence reflects only firms' own adjustment frictions or also the past financing choices of economically connected firms. We combine annual firm fundamentals with time-varying text-based product-market networks and estimate a heterogeneous dynamic partial-adjustment model with interactive effects using defactored instrumental variables. The estimator accommodates time- varying network weights and spatial dependence in firm-specific coefficients. Network-weighted lagged leverage is positive and statistically significant, with a mean coefficient representing approximately 45% of the sum of the own and network lag coefficients for book leverage. Accounting for network dependence reduces the persistence attributed to firms' own financing histories and increases the implied own-firm speed of adjustment. Firm-specific estimates reveal significant product-market clustering in own-leverage persistence and in responses to several leverage determinants, showing that heterogeneity in financing behaviour is systematically related to product-market proximity. The evolution of product-market connections matters quantitatively for network dependence: holding the network fixed produces a substantially larger network coefficient and considerably larger indirect effects than using annual network weights. Network dependence is therefore an economically important component of leverage dynamics, while its measurement depends on both the specification of economic connections and heterogeneity in firm behaviour.
item.dc:creator: Stylianos Asimakopoulos, Vasilis Sarafidis

item.title: Siting and Curtailment Depth Limit the Grid Headroom Available to New Large Loads
item.description: arXiv:2611.00462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data center demand is increasing faster than generation can be built, encouraging proposals to interconnect large loads on condition that they reduce consumption during high-stress periods. Estimates of how much load can be added via flexibility rest on simplified accounting and report only annual curtailed electricity. Here we use a national energy systems model that co-optimizes hourly generation and load curtailment across 16 U.S. regions to characterize the flexibility and power system impacts of enabling headroom. While 50 GW can be served while curtailing less than 0.1% of its annual energy, small annual curtailment conceals potentially severe operating requirements. Most regions require curtailment deeper than 90% in at least one hour, so the load must disconnect or have sufficient on-site resources to provide full back up. Furthermore, announced data center locations are not aligned with modeled headroom and relying on existing generation fleets raises CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity prices.
item.dc:creator: Nils Johnson, Geoff Blanford, John E. T. Bistline

item.title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
item.description: arXiv:2611.00661v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. A profile-generation LLM assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the learning data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11-20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.
item.dc:creator: Robin Na, Kehang Zhu, Logan Cross, Michiel A. Bakker

item.title: Agent-Based Disruption Simulation on an Edge-Level Product-Annotated Supply Network of the Automotive Industry
item.description: arXiv:2611.01706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Disruptions spread through supply networks when customers cannot replace the products they lose. We ask how portfolio-overlap and product-specific rules for selecting candidate suppliers change cascades when customers search for new suppliers and form new supply edges. From the MarkLines database, we construct a product-annotated network of about 77,000 firms and 197,000 supplier-customer edges in the global automotive industry. We extend an agent-based disruption model with edge-level products, a product-specific substitution rule based on the semantic similarity of product names, and calibrated capacities and inventories. Only 6% of the edges carry observed products. We impute the others and test the imputation against the annotated edges. We run 119,000 simulations. With all other mechanics fixed, the product-specific rule makes the cascades after a hub failure four to five times larger than the portfolio-overlap rule of the original model. Under alternative imputations and similarity thresholds, the factor ranges from 1.2 to 18. Within the simulations, substitutability also shapes which suppliers are critical. Network topology largely determines which firms a shock reaches, and substitutability determines how many of them fail. Of the 50 most damaging suppliers under random disruptions, topology alone identifies 20 and an index that adds product substitutability identifies 32. The index carries over without refitting to a regional scenario modelled on the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake. Supply network risk assessment should account for product-level substitutability and therefore needs product data on supply relationships.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Rolf, Hiroyasu Inoue, Sebastian Lang

item.title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
item.description: arXiv:2611.01750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Herfindahl--Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration, is widely used to quantify competitive balance in sports tournaments. To enable comparisons over time or across leagues, both its minimum and maximum should be known. The minimum is usually trivial. Our paper provides results on the maximum HHI in incomplete round-robin tournaments, where the set of matches is represented by a regular but not complete undirected graph. We prove that the lower bound of maximum HHI is reached when the tournament consists of independent round-robin groups, while the upper bound of maximum HHI is reached when the set of matches is represented by a bipartite graph. Maximising HHI is computationally difficult even for highly structured graph types corresponding to real-world tournaments, where the teams are partitioned into pots and play the same number of matches against opponents from every pot. The complexity of the problem does not depend on the scoring system or the number of opponents from a pot.
item.dc:creator: Gergely Cs\'aji, L\'aszl\'o Csat\'o

item.title: How Green Is Your Manifesto? Scoring Environmental Positions in the 2024 EU Elections with an LLM Panel
item.description: arXiv:2611.02033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Locating political parties on environmental and climate policy is central to the study of party competition, yet the established instruments, expert surveys and the hand coding of manifestos, are costly, periodic, and slow to extend to new documents. We ask whether a panel of large language models can serve as a cheaper and reproducible alternative. Treating each manifesto as a set of sentences, three models from independent providers score every sentence on two dimensions, environmental protection and climate change, separating a party's position on an issue from the salience it gives it, and the judgments are averaged to the manifesto level. Agreement across the models is retained as a built-in reliability signal. We apply the panel to 41 manifestos from the 2024 European Parliament election, covering Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the European party families, and validate it against the 2024 Chapel Hill Expert Survey for the 25 parties with a like-for-like expert benchmark, using the other manifestos as diagnostic cases. The panel recovers the expert ordering of parties with strong rank agreement on both dimensions, while reading them as systematically greener than experts do, a gap we interpret as the distance between manifesto promise and governing record. Inter-model disagreement modestly flags where the instrument errs, and position and salience prove related for environmental protection but independent for climate change. The result is a transparent, low-cost, and multilingual instrument that complements rather than replaces expert and hand-coded approaches; the prompt, code, and manifesto-level results are released openly.
item.dc:creator: Franco Corti, Sajid Siraj

item.title: Ask More, Hear Less: How a Review Prompt Changes What Online Ratings Show
item.description: arXiv:2611.02623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Platforms ask customers for online reviews to reduce self-selection, but theory conflicts on whether review solicitation makes online ratings more or less informative. Selection theory implies that asking helps, voice theory that it dilutes the news, and research on rating inflation that compression destroys information. We reconcile these views with signal detection theory, which separates what a rating knows (its sensitivity) from what it shows (its criterion). We test the framework on Steam, a leading PC video game store, whose client began in October 2019 to prompt players for a review after about three hours of play. Using a difference-in-discontinuities design at that inferred threshold in 21.6 million Steam reviews of 315 games, we find that review counts just above the threshold become 4.25 times those just below, and the jump in the positive share grows by 6.6 percentage points. Agreement with critics changes little near launch and erodes later. The rating's movement changes far more: pass-through from reviews written in the first two hours falls from 0.73 to 0.18 just above the threshold, against 0.81 to 0.64 just below, and a fixed rating tier responds to 12% of downturns in those reviews above the threshold, down from 42%, against 41% and 47% below it. What the stream knows changes less. At equal review counts its sensitivity falls more above the threshold, because added reviews respond about half as much and scores near the ceiling are noisier per review, but at natural counts added volume offsets this loss, leaving a change of -0.03 relative to the stream below (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06). Failures that developers acknowledge, which run through complaints, still move the score after launch. Review prompts therefore mainly change how a rating must be read, and platforms that solicit reviews should recalibrate their rating labels.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu

item.title: Learning to Charge More: How Q-Learning Firms Lock In Supracompetitive Prices
item.description: arXiv:2505.22909v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There is growing experimental evidence that $Q$-learning agents can learn to charge supracompetitive prices. We ask when such behavior persists, whether it emerges, and which strategies support it. In a repeated pricing game in which firms condition on the previous period's price profile, we give conditions on the learned action values under which supracompetitive prices become an absorbing state once experimentation ends. We then show that under softmax exploration these conditions are reached with positive and explicitly bounded probability, both from a random and from an all-zero initial $Q$-table. In the latter case firms lock in supracompetitive prices because they never learn that undercutting pays; the same mechanism can lock in the competitive price, so the long-run outcome is selected by the exploration path. Finally, we give sufficient conditions on the learned table under which the induced strategy is naive collusion, a grim trigger strategy or an increasing-price strategy; grim trigger strategies are subgame perfect under a standard discounting condition, whereas naive collusion is generally not an equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Cristian Chica, Yinglong Guo, Gilad Lerman

item.title: From macro to micro: Economic complexity indicators for firm growth
item.description: arXiv:2507.21754v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A rich theoretical and empirical literature has investigated the link between export diversification and firm performance. Prior theoretical works hinted at the key role of capability accumulation in shaping production activities and performance, without however producing product-level indicators able to forecast corporate growth. Building on economic complexity theory and the corporate growth literature, this paper examines which characteristics of a firm's export basket anticipate future performance. We analyze a unique longitudinal dataset that covers export and financial data for 57,586 Italian firms. We find that firms exporting products typically exported by wealthier countries -- a proxy for products characterized by a greater level of productivity and sophistication -- tend to experience higher growth and labour productivity. Crucially, where firms diversify matters: Across firms, only diversification outside of a firm's core export area is positively associated with future growth, whereas diversification within the core is negatively associated. This is revealed by introducing novel measures of in-block and out-of-block export diversification, based on algorithmically-detected blocks. Our findings suggest that growth is associated not just with how many products a firm exports, but also with where these products lie within the production ecosystem, at both local and global scales.
item.dc:creator: Maddalena Mula, Valerio De Stefano, Manuel Sebastian Mariani, Andrea Zaccaria

item.title: AI and the research assistant: Evidence from economics working papers
item.description: arXiv:2608.08437v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Studies of AI in science observe isolated tasks or the authors on a byline. They do not observe the research assistants whose data cleaning, coding, literature search, and replication work language models now perform. Economics working papers record this junior labour in their acknowledgements, next to the full text. Using 24 working-paper series through October 2026, I compare papers by the same economist that do and do not disclose AI use, alongside a detector of AI-like prose. Disclosing papers credit 0.548 more named assistants than other papers by the same economist, two-thirds of the mean, and run longer, mostly in their appendices. Disclosures of operational use, such as coding and data work, carry the whole assistant difference; writing-only disclosures and AI-like prose show no consistent association with assistants or pages. The paper brings acknowledged junior labour and selective team disclosure into the study of scientific production. Within an economist's portfolio, operational AI accompanies wider, assistant-supported projects.
item.dc:creator: Johan Fourie

item.title: The Price of Intelligence: A Quality-Adjusted Price Index for AI Services
item.description: arXiv:2608.29843v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How fast AI inference prices have fallen depends on how an index holds quality constant. We build quality-adjusted price indices for text and code inference sold through APIs, joining 21,024 posted prices to a capability scale fitted to 4,605 benchmark scores. From January 2025 to July 2026, matched-model methods record an annual fall of 0.07 in log price per token. Our pre-specified hedonic index falls at 0.51 a year in logs (95% interval 0.11 to 0.89), entirely through the rising capability of the models on sale. Across three treatments of measurement error and two anchor sets it runs from 0.34 to 0.89. Excluding six anchors flagged for possible contamination leaves model rankings intact (rank correlation 0.998) yet lowers the rate by 0.40 to 0.51 under two treatments. Agreement on rankings therefore does not license claims about levels or increments. Per completed task, the data do not establish a quality-adjusted decline.
item.dc:creator: Louis Yiven Zhu

item.title: MOE-DGSCND: Multi-Objective Enterprise Green Supply Chain Network Design
item.description: arXiv:2609.11971v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces and studies the Multi-Objective Enterprise Doubly-Green Supply Chain Network Design (MOE-DGSCND) problem, an extension of Multi-Objective Supply Chain Network Design. The problem studied here is a three-objective combinatorial optimization problem that simultaneously minimizes total cost f1, carbon dioxide emissions f2 and customer dissatisfaction f3 over binary decisions regarding which distribution centers to open and how to assign customer zones to open facilities. The problem generalizes the capacitated facility location problem (CFLP) and is known to be NP-hard (Garey and Johnson, 1979). This paper formally specifies the decision variables, objective functions and constraints and investigates three solution approaches using a single numerical instance: (A) an exact weighted-sum integer linear programming (ILP) formulation solved with Python combinatorially and via PuLP, (B) three Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes (FPTAS) providing (1 + $\epsilon$)-approximate solutions for $\epsilon$ := 0.15 and (C) two baseline heuristics for comparison. On an instance with eight customers and five candidate distribution centers, the exact solver certifies the optimal (sampled) supported solutions across eight weight combinations, while the FPTAS-based approaches complete within milliseconds, compared to centiseconds for the exact ILP on this tiny non-stochastic instance.
item.dc:creator: Felix Reichel

item.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
item.description: arXiv:2610.30858v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI systems are increasingly used to complete economically valuable tasks in various professions, such as software engineering and finance. This motivates the question: how much economic value does an AI system produce per unit of energy? To answer it, we introduce Joules-to-GDP, a framework that measures output dollar value minus AI execution cost per unit of energy, which we call Net Value per Joule (NVJ), and expert time saved per unit of energy, or Time Saving per Joule (TSJ). We then apply the framework to 220 GDPval tasks across 44 occupations. Four findings stand out. First, the most valuable work is not always the most efficient. For example, engineering work such as CAD design yields about 10% more net value per task than software development such as building websites, yet the latter yields about 27% more per joule. Second, defaulting to the most capable model can mean less total value from the same energy budget. Of the five tested models, GLM 5.2 delivers the most net value, $72.27 per task on average, using the energy of about four hours of active laptop use, while Gemma 4 31B achieves 56% of that with 23% of the energy, for 2.5x the NVJ and 2.8x the TSJ. Third, for the same model, NVJ and TSJ vary widely across different accelerators, and adding GPUs can raise energy use for modest gains: eight H100s use 3.2x the energy of one to cut completion time by only 22%, at similar net value. More capable models and more hardware must therefore earn their extra energy with enough gains in output value. Finally, the work of experts who use AI is harder for AI to match than that of experts working alone. Measured against it, GLM 5.2's NVJ falls by 70% and its TSJ by 65%. Taken together, these findings justify economic return per joule as an objective for selecting professional tasks and improving language models and accelerators, and as a basis for examining AI's effect on the economy
